front: What is the continuous Cost-of-Carry formula for a simple financial asset with no dividends?
back: F = S × e^(rT), where F is the futures price, S is the current spot price, r is the annual risk-free rate, and T is time to expiration in years.

front: How does an expected dividend yield (q) alter the continuous futures pricing formula?
back: F = S × e^((r - q)T). Because futures holders do not receive dividends, expected dividend yields lower the net cost of carry, reducing the theoretical futures price.
A market condition where the futures price is higher than the current spot price (F > S), creating an upward-sloping futures price curve over time.
A market condition where the futures price is lower than the current spot price (F < S), often caused by high dividend yields (q > r) or high convenience yields in commodities.
The process where the futures price gradually equals the spot price (F = S) as time to contract expiration approaches zero (T → 0).

front: Why must futures prices converge to spot prices at contract expiry?
back: At expiration, futures contracts turn into immediate spot delivery. Any price difference (F ≠ S) creates instantaneous risk-free arbitrage that forces prices together.
